FAQ

The questions you would ask on the third call.

The product pages answer what it does. This one answers what happens to you if we get it wrong, go under, get bought, or turn out to be smaller than you hoped. Every answer here is the one we would give on a call, including the ones that cost us the deal.

Nothing on this page is a promise that only exists on this page. Where an answer is contractual we say so, because a commitment on a marketing page is worth exactly what a marketing page is worth. The terms are readable on this site before you talk to anyone.

If something happens to us

What if you disappear?

The honest structure of the risk: Ordence is a small, founder-led company built by Sahil Nahar, and small companies do fail. What protects you is not a promise, it is a design decision. Your statutory books stay in Tally on purpose, so the documents an auditor asks for by name never lived only with us. Your operational data is exportable in open formats at any time, without asking and without a ticket. There is no source-code escrow arrangement and we are not going to pretend one would help — a business of thirty people cannot run a codebase it was handed. What you can actually do is leave with your data and be running elsewhere, and that route is tested by the fact that customers use the export routinely, not only on the way out.

What happens if you get acquired?

It can happen and we will not claim otherwise. Two things matter. Your export rights and the commitment that your workspace is never training data are in the terms, not in a blog post, and terms survive a change of control. And your practical protection is unchanged: if the new owner takes it somewhere you do not want to go, you export and leave. If we are ever in that conversation, customers hear before the announcement, not from it.

Why should we trust a company nobody has heard of?

Do not trust us. Check us. The security page lists what we have not built, including no SOC 2 and no penetration test report. The compare page names four alternatives and says when to buy them instead. There is no logo wall on this site and no invented testimonial, and the worked example is labelled a composite because it is one. That is the whole of what we can offer at this size, and if it is not enough, Zoho and SAP have been around for decades and that is a legitimate reason to buy from them.

Can we speak to a customer?

Ask on a call and we will see who is willing. We are small enough that the honest answer some months is that nobody in a comparable business is free that week, and we would rather say that than manufacture a reference. What we will do instead is put your real data in a workspace and let you use it.

Your data

Who owns the data?

You do. Under the DPDP Act you are the data fiduciary for the personal data in your workspace and we process it on your instruction. We do not sell it, we do not train models on it, and we do not use one customer's records to improve another customer's experience. That last one is contractual, not a preference.

Can we get our data out?

Yes. Open formats, whenever you want, without asking us and without a support ticket — including while an invoice to us is overdue, which is the moment most vendors quietly turn the tap off. After an agreement ends you have thirty days to take anything else, and then we delete our copies.

What if we want to move to SAP or Odoo later?

Then you should, and the export is real. The uncomfortable part: nobody's export is a turnkey import into anything. You will pay an implementation partner to map our fields to theirs, and that work is real work. What we do is hand over the schema documentation with the data instead of making them reverse-engineer a CSV, and answer their questions during the transition without charging for it.

What if we outgrow you?

Name the edges, so you can see them coming. Multiple legal entities being consolidated, more than one country or currency, material requirements planning, shop-floor scheduling, or a procurement process that requires SOC 2 or ISO 27001. Hit any of those and the right answer is SAP Business One or Odoo with a partner, and we will say so rather than build a bad version of it for you. We would rather lose a customer to growth than keep one badly served.

People

What if our accountant refuses?

Very common, usually reasonable, and almost always about a specific fear: that somebody is about to take Tally away. Nobody is. Ordence exports vouchers into Tally with deterministic identifiers so a re-export updates rather than duplicates, and the statutory books stay exactly where your auditor expects them. Get your CA onto the second call, not the tenth — they will ask sharper questions than you will, and if they still object after seeing the Tally export and the GSTR-2B reconciliation, that objection is information. Sometimes they are protecting a workflow. Sometimes they are right that you are not ready.

Do you work with our CA?

Yes, and we prefer it. The division is deliberate: Ordence prepares, reconciles and evidences. Your CA reviews and files. We do not submit anything to GSTN or the income tax portal, we do not hold your portal credentials, and we do not want them. Your CA gets an ITC register in the shape GSTR-3B Table 4 wants, a TDS register with the statutory reference on every row, and a Tally export.

What if the person who set it up leaves our company?

This is the most common quiet failure in this whole category, and it is worth planning against rather than hoping. Three things we insist on. Configuration lives in the workspace and not in one person's head, so nothing is lost when they go. The written scope says what was built and why, and you keep it. And we ask for two named people from your side from day one, not one — a champion and a deputy. If your champion leaves, we retrain their replacement without charging for it.

What does support actually mean from a team this small?

Concretely: email to one inbox, and a phone number in your agreement. Read by the people who built the product, usually the same day. Something that has stopped your business working gets looked at the same day. The uncomfortable half — there is no 24-hour desk, no follow-the-sun rota, and no published uptime SLA with service credits, because we do not have enough operating history for that number to mean anything. Occasionally you will wait a few hours longer than you would from a large vendor. It also means the person replying can change the thing you are complaining about, that week.

Money and commitment

How long until we see value?

First module in genuine daily use in weeks, not months. The first measurable change is usually not revenue and we would distrust anyone who promised it was — it is that no enquiry sits unanswered over a weekend, or that the stock number is right on a Wednesday. Month-end shortening is a quarter's worth of work, because it needs the ledger, the reconciliation and people's habits all to have moved.

Can we start with one module?

Yes, and it is usually the better path. The CRM works alone. The ERP works alone. Start where it hurts most, get people actually using it, then add. A launch across every department at once is the single most reliable way to fail at this, and we have talked customers out of it.

Can we pause?

Not mid-term, and this is the least comfortable answer on the page. There is an initial term. Fees paid for a term you leave part-way through are not refunded, because our costs for that term are already committed. If we are the ones ending it, the unused part comes back to you. What we can do in practice is adjust user count at renewal and, by agreement, move a workspace to a read-only state rather than have you pay for seats nobody is using. That is a conversation, not a button.

What if the scope turns out to be wrong?

Small changes — a field, a report, a rule, a document template — are part of the subscription and we do not bill for them. Anything larger gets a written change note with a price on it before we build it, never after. If the scope was wrong because we misunderstood your business, that correction is on us and we say so in writing.

We tried a system like this before and it failed. Why would this be different?

Ask why it failed, because the reason is usually one of three and only one of them is about the software. It went live across every department at once. The data went in dirty and people stopped believing the screens. Or nobody on your side owned it, so it became the vendor's project. If it was the third one, we cannot fix that and neither can any other vendor — the process page says exactly what we need from you and when, so you can decide before signing whether you have that person.

Short answers to the rest

Asked often enough to be worth a line each.

  • No free trial and no self-serve signup. Every customer is a written scope and a fixed quote, deliberately.
  • No per-seat price list on the site, because two businesses of the same headcount can be four times apart in the work.
  • India only. Not multi-country, not multi-currency, and that is a choice rather than a gap we are racing to close.
  • If we have no capacity until a given month we will tell you that instead of taking your money and being late.
  • If what you need is a better spreadsheet and a tighter process, we will say so. It has happened more than once.

Ask the one that is actually stopping you.

It is usually not on this page, and it is usually not about features. Send it and you will get the same answer we would give on a call.
